nodes.desc: For products and quotients the percent uncertainties add (to first order), which bounds the uncertainty of a result.

nodes.label: Significant figures
nodes.desc: Bookkeeping rule that keeps only the digits supported by the uncertainty of the inputs.

nodes.label: Scalar
nodes.desc: A quantity fixed by one real number and a unit; scalars obey ordinary arithmetic.

nodes.label: Vector
nodes.desc: A quantity with magnitude and direction; displacement is the model case. Two vectors can be parallel, antiparallel or orthogonal.

nodes.label: Vector addition
nodes.desc: Combines vectors head to tail (or by the parallelogram) into a resultant; subtraction adds the antiparallel vector.

nodes.label: Multiplication by a scalar
nodes.desc: Stretches a vector by |α| and reverses it if α < 0; dividing a vector by its magnitude gives a unit vector.

nodes.label: Vector components
nodes.desc: Writes a vector in the orthonormal basis of a Cartesian coordinate system; vector equations become one scalar equation per axis.

nodes.label: Polar coordinates
nodes.desc: Locates a point in a plane by its distance from the origin and an angle from the x-axis.

nodes.label: Scalar product
nodes.desc: Multiplies two vectors into a scalar, AB cos φ; it projects one vector on another and vanishes for orthogonal vectors.

nodes.label: Vector product
nodes.desc: Multiplies two vectors into a vector perpendicular to both, of magnitude AB sin φ, oriented by the right-hand rule.

nodes.label: Position
nodes.desc: Coordinate of the body on an axis of the frame at a given instant.

nodes.label: Reference frame
nodes.desc: An origin and axes against which positions are measured, together with a clock.

nodes.label: Motion on a line
nodes.desc: The kinematic state of a body on a line: its position at every instant.

nodes.label: Displacement
nodes.desc: Change of position between two instants; signed. A total displacement is the sum of successive displacements.

nodes.label: Distance traveled
nodes.desc: Total length of path covered, never negative; it can exceed the magnitude of the displacement.

nodes.label: Average velocity
nodes.desc: Displacement divided by the elapsed time; it depends only on the end points of the interval.

nodes.label: Elapsed time
nodes.desc: Duration of an interval between two clock readings.

nodes.label: Time derivative
nodes.desc: The limit of a difference quotient as the interval shrinks; turns a quantity known at every instant into its rate of change.

nodes.label: Instantaneous velocity
nodes.desc: Rate of change of position at an instant: the slope of x(t).

nodes.label: Average speed
nodes.desc: Distance traveled divided by elapsed time.

nodes.label: Speed
nodes.desc: Magnitude of the instantaneous velocity.

nodes.label: Average acceleration
nodes.desc: Change of velocity divided by elapsed time.

nodes.label: Instantaneous acceleration
nodes.desc: Rate of change of velocity: the slope of v(t) and the second derivative of x(t), which sets the concavity of its graph.

nodes.label: Constant-acceleration kinematics
nodes.desc: The motion when acceleration does not change: velocity linear and position quadratic in time.

nodes.label: Free fall
nodes.desc: Vertical motion with acceleration −g; Galileo's result that the motion does not depend on the mass.

nodes.label: Free-fall acceleration
nodes.desc: Acceleration of a body falling near Earth's surface without air resistance: about 9.80 m/s², the same for all bodies at one place.

nodes.label: Time integral
nodes.desc: Accumulates a rate over time; undoes the derivative up to a constant fixed by initial conditions.

nodes.label: Position vector
nodes.desc: Vector from the origin of the frame to the body: r⃗ = x î + y ĵ + z k̂.

nodes.label: Trajectory
nodes.desc: The kinematic state in space: the curve traced by the position vector, made of three independent motions along the axes.

nodes.label: Displacement vector
nodes.desc: Change of the position vector between two instants.

nodes.label: Velocity vector
nodes.desc: Rate of change of the position vector; tangent to the trajectory.

nodes.label: Acceleration vector
nodes.desc: Rate of change of the velocity vector; in curved motion it has parts across and along the path (total acceleration).

nodes.label: Projectile motion
nodes.desc: Motion under gravity alone: uniform horizontally, free fall vertically, the two independent.

nodes.label: Time of flight
nodes.desc: Time a projectile spends in the air.

nodes.label: Range
nodes.desc: Horizontal distance traveled by a projectile landing at its launch height.

nodes.label: Circular motion
nodes.desc: The state of a body moving on a circle of radius r: its angle at every instant.

nodes.label: Centripetal acceleration
nodes.desc: Acceleration toward the centre needed to keep a body on a circle.

nodes.label: Angular frequency
nodes.desc: Rate at which the angle advances, in rad/s; constant in uniform circular motion.

nodes.label: Tangential acceleration
nodes.desc: Rate of change of speed; directed along the path.

nodes.label: Relative motion
nodes.desc: Converts positions and velocities between two reference frames in relative motion by adding the frames' relative position and velocity.

nodes.label: Relative velocity
nodes.desc: Velocity of a body measured in a frame that itself moves.

nodes.label: Force
nodes.desc: A push or pull on a body, with magnitude and direction; measured by the stretch of a calibrated spring. SI unit the newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

nodes.label: Free-body diagram
nodes.desc: Isolates one body and draws every external force on it as a vector from the body; the starting point of every force problem.

nodes.label: Net external force
nodes.desc: Vector sum of all external forces on a body.

nodes.label: Newton's first law
nodes.desc: A body keeps its velocity unless a net external force acts; this tendency is inertia, measured by mass.

nodes.label: Inertial reference frame
nodes.desc: A frame in which the first law holds; any frame moving at constant velocity relative to one is also inertial.

nodes.label: Newton's second law
nodes.desc: The net external force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; one equation per component.

nodes.label: Weight
nodes.desc: Gravitational force of the Earth on a body near its surface; proportional to mass, unlike mass itself it depends on location.

nodes.label: Newton's third law
nodes.desc: Forces come in pairs: when A pushes on B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. The two act on different bodies.

nodes.label: Normal force
nodes.desc: Contact force perpendicular to a surface, as large as needed to stop the body from moving into it.

nodes.label: Tension
nodes.desc: Pulling force transmitted along a string or cable.

nodes.label: Hooke's law
nodes.desc: A spring pulls back with a force proportional to its stretch from the relaxed length.

nodes.label: Friction law
nodes.desc: Contact force parallel to a surface that opposes relative motion (kinetic) or its onset (static), proportional to the normal force.

nodes.label: Static friction
nodes.desc: Friction between surfaces not sliding relative to each other; adjusts up to a maximum μ_s N.

nodes.label: Kinetic friction
nodes.desc: Friction between sliding surfaces, opposite to the relative velocity.

nodes.label: Centripetal force
nodes.desc: Net force toward the centre that a circular motion requires; supplied by tension, friction, gravity or a normal force.

nodes.label: Banked curve
nodes.desc: A road tilted so the horizontal part of the normal force supplies the centripetal force at a design speed.

nodes.label: Noninertial frame
nodes.desc: An accelerating or rotating frame; the laws of motion hold there only if inertial (fictitious) forces such as the centrifugal force are added.

nodes.label: Coriolis force
nodes.desc: Inertial force on a body moving relative to a rotating frame, perpendicular to its velocity; deflects winds and projectiles on Earth.

nodes.label: Drag force
nodes.desc: Resistance of a fluid to a body moving through it; grows with the square of speed for fast motion, linearly for slow motion in viscous fluid.

nodes.label: Terminal velocity
nodes.desc: Constant speed reached when the drag force balances the weight.

nodes.label: Work
nodes.desc: Energy transferred by a force acting along a displacement; only the component of force along the path does work. SI unit the joule.

nodes.label: Kinetic energy
nodes.desc: Energy of motion of a particle; depends on the frame through the speed.

nodes.label: Net work
nodes.desc: Work done by the net force, equal to the sum of the works of all forces.

nodes.label: Work–energy theorem
nodes.desc: The net work done on a particle equals its change of kinetic energy.

nodes.label: Power
nodes.desc: Rate at which work is done; P = F⃗·v⃗ for a force acting on a moving body. Average power is work over elapsed time.

nodes.label: Potential energy
nodes.desc: Energy of a system stored in its configuration; only differences are physical, so the zero can be chosen freely.

nodes.label: Gravitational potential energy (near Earth)
nodes.desc: Potential energy of the body–Earth system for a height y near the surface.

nodes.label: Elastic potential energy
nodes.desc: Potential energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring.

nodes.label: Conservative force
nodes.desc: A force whose work between two points is independent of the path; equivalently zero around every closed path, and derivable from a potential energy.

nodes.label: Work of nonconservative forces
nodes.desc: Work by forces such as friction or air resistance, which depends on the path and changes the mechanical energy.

nodes.label: Mechanical energy
nodes.desc: Kinetic plus potential energy of a system.

nodes.label: Conservation of mechanical energy
nodes.desc: Mechanical energy changes only through the work of nonconservative forces; without them it is a conserved quantity.

nodes.label: Potential-energy diagram
nodes.desc: A plot of U(x) with the total energy as a horizontal line; motion is allowed only where E ≥ U, and reverses at turning points.

nodes.label: Equilibrium point
nodes.desc: A position where the force vanishes; stable at a minimum of U (small disturbances oscillate), unstable at a maximum.

nodes.label: Momentum
nodes.desc: Mass times velocity; a vector.

nodes.label: Impulse
nodes.desc: Time integral of a force; for a short collision, average force times duration.

nodes.label: Impulse–momentum theorem
nodes.desc: The impulse of the net force equals the change of momentum.

nodes.label: System of particles
nodes.desc: A chosen set of bodies; forces split into internal (between members) and external. A closed system has no net external force.

nodes.label: Conservation of momentum
nodes.desc: The total momentum of a closed system does not change, whatever happens inside it.

nodes.label: Collisions
nodes.desc: Collisions conserve momentum; they are classified by kinetic energy: elastic (kept), inelastic (lost), perfectly inelastic (bodies stick together), explosion (gained).

nodes.label: Center of mass
nodes.desc: Mass-weighted average position of a system; for a continuous body r⃗_CM = (1/M)∫ r⃗ dm.

nodes.label: Second law for a system
nodes.desc: The centre of mass moves like a single particle of total mass M acted on by the external forces alone.

nodes.label: Linear mass density
nodes.desc: Mass per unit length of a rod or string; used to integrate over continuous bodies.

nodes.label: Rocket equation
nodes.desc: A rocket gains speed by ejecting mass backward at exhaust speed u; the gain depends on the logarithm of the mass ratio.

nodes.label: Rigid body on a fixed axis
nodes.desc: A body whose particles keep their mutual distances, turning about a fixed axis: every particle moves on a circle and one angle describes them all.

nodes.label: Angular position
nodes.desc: Angle of a reference line of the body from a fixed direction, in radians: arc length over radius.

nodes.label: Angular velocity
nodes.desc: Rate of change of angular position; as a vector it points along the axis by the right-hand rule. Tangential speed v_t = rω.

nodes.label: Angular acceleration
nodes.desc: Rate of change of angular velocity; tangential acceleration of a point is a_t = rα.

nodes.label: Rotational kinematics
nodes.desc: Equations for rotation at constant angular acceleration, the same form as the linear ones with θ, ω, α in place of x, v, a.

nodes.label: Rotational kinetic energy
nodes.desc: Kinetic energy of a rotating rigid body, the sum of ½m_j v_j² with v_j = r_{j}ω.

nodes.label: Moment of inertia
nodes.desc: Rotational inertia: how mass is distributed about the axis. Depends on the axis chosen.

nodes.label: Parallel-axis theorem
nodes.desc: The moment of inertia about any axis equals that about the parallel axis through the centre of mass plus Md².

nodes.label: Surface mass density
nodes.desc: Mass per unit area of a thin sheet or disk.

nodes.label: Torque
nodes.desc: The turning effect of a force about a point or axis: force times lever arm, |τ| = r⊥F, signed by the right-hand rule.

nodes.label: Second law for rotation
nodes.desc: Net torque about a fixed axis equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

nodes.label: Rotational work
nodes.desc: Work done by a torque as the body turns.

nodes.label: Rolling without slipping
nodes.desc: A wheel rolls without slipping when its contact point is instantaneously at rest; translation and rotation are then locked together.

nodes.label: Angular momentum
nodes.desc: Moment of momentum about a point; for a rigid body rotating about a symmetry axis, L = Iω.

nodes.label: Torque law
nodes.desc: The rate of change of angular momentum equals the net external torque.

nodes.label: Conservation of angular momentum
nodes.desc: With no net external torque, the total angular momentum is constant; a skater who pulls in her arms (smaller I) spins faster.

nodes.label: Precession rate
nodes.desc: Slow turning of a spinning top's axis, because gravity's torque changes the direction of L⃗ rather than its size.

nodes.label: Static equilibrium
nodes.desc: A rigid body at rest that stays at rest; it has no translational and no rotational acceleration.

nodes.label: Equilibrium conditions
nodes.desc: The first condition (zero net force) prevents translation; the second (zero net torque) prevents rotation.

nodes.label: Center of gravity
nodes.desc: Point where the total weight can be taken to act; it coincides with the centre of mass in a uniform gravitational field.

nodes.label: Stress
nodes.desc: Force per unit area that deforms a body: tensile or compressive (perpendicular), bulk (from all sides), shear (parallel to the surface).

nodes.label: Strain
nodes.desc: Fractional deformation: change of length, volume or shear offset divided by the original size; dimensionless.

nodes.label: Linear elasticity
nodes.desc: For small deformations stress is proportional to strain; the constant is the elastic modulus of the material for that kind of deformation.

nodes.label: Young's modulus
nodes.desc: Elastic modulus for tension or compression along one direction.

nodes.label: Bulk modulus
nodes.desc: Elastic modulus for uniform compression; its inverse is the compressibility.

nodes.label: Shear modulus
nodes.desc: Elastic modulus for shear deformation.

nodes.label: Pressure
nodes.desc: Perpendicular force per unit area; a scalar. SI unit the pascal, 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

nodes.label: Stress–strain diagram
nodes.desc: A material is linear up to the proportionality limit, elastic (returns to shape) up to the elastic limit, plastic beyond it, and breaks at the ultimate stress.

nodes.label: Gravitational constant
nodes.desc: Strength of gravity between two masses, 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², first measured with a torsion balance (Cavendish).

nodes.label: Newton's law of gravitation
nodes.desc: Every pair of point masses attracts along the line joining them with a force proportional to both masses and inversely to the square of the distance.

nodes.label: Gravitational field
nodes.desc: Gravitational force per unit mass at a point; it exists whether or not a test mass is there.

nodes.label: Apparent weight
nodes.desc: What a scale reads: the normal force, which differs from mg in an accelerating or rotating frame (reduced at the equator by Earth's rotation).

nodes.label: Gravitational potential energy
nodes.desc: Potential energy of two masses at any separation, with zero at infinite separation; near Earth's surface it reduces to mgy.

nodes.label: Escape velocity
nodes.desc: Minimum launch speed for a body to move off to infinite distance.

nodes.label: Gravitationally bound orbit
nodes.desc: A system whose total energy is negative cannot separate to infinity; the bodies stay within a maximum distance.

nodes.label: Orbital speed
nodes.desc: Speed of a circular orbit at radius r; independent of the satellite's mass.

nodes.label: Orbital period
nodes.desc: Time for one circular orbit.

nodes.label: Kepler's first law
nodes.desc: Every planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; derived by Newton from the inverse-square law.

nodes.label: Elliptical orbit
nodes.desc: The orbital state: an ellipse traced periodically, closest to the Sun at perihelion and farthest at aphelion.

nodes.label: Kepler's second law
nodes.desc: The line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest at perihelion.

nodes.label: Kepler's third law
nodes.desc: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis.

nodes.label: Tidal force
nodes.desc: Difference in the gravitational pull across a body; it stretches the body along the line to the attracting mass. Sun and Moon aligned give spring tides, at right angles neap tides.

nodes.label: Speed of light
nodes.desc: Speed of light in vacuum, exactly 299 792 458 m/s by the definition of the metre (≈ 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s).

nodes.label: General relativity
nodes.desc: Gravity is the curvature of space-time produced by mass and energy; free bodies follow the straightest paths of the curved geometry.

nodes.label: Principle of equivalence
nodes.desc: No local experiment can distinguish a uniform gravitational field from an accelerated frame; a freely falling frame is locally inertial.

nodes.label: Black hole
nodes.desc: A mass compressed inside its Schwarzschild radius; nothing, not even light, escapes from inside the event horizon.

nodes.label: Schwarzschild radius
nodes.desc: Radius at which the escape velocity from a mass M reaches the speed of light; it marks the event horizon.

nodes.label: Fluid
nodes.desc: A liquid or gas: matter that flows because it cannot resist a shear stress when at rest; described by fields such as density and pressure.

nodes.label: Density
nodes.desc: Mass per unit volume.

nodes.label: Specific gravity
nodes.desc: Density relative to that of water; dimensionless.

nodes.label: Gauge and absolute pressure
nodes.desc: Gauges read pressure relative to the atmosphere; absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure.

nodes.label: Hydrostatic equilibrium
nodes.desc: In a fluid at rest pressure grows with depth so that each fluid element is balanced: p = p₀ + ρgh for constant density.

nodes.label: Pascal's principle
nodes.desc: A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid reaches every part of it; a hydraulic jack multiplies force by the area ratio.

nodes.label: Buoyant force
nodes.desc: Net upward force of a fluid on an immersed body.

nodes.label: Archimedes' principle
nodes.desc: A body immersed in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

nodes.label: Ideal fluid
nodes.desc: A model fluid with constant density and no internal friction; its steady flow is laminar.

nodes.label: Viscosity
nodes.desc: Internal friction of a fluid: the shear stress needed per velocity gradient.

nodes.label: Fluid flow
nodes.desc: The motion of a fluid: a velocity at every point. In laminar flow the layers slide smoothly; in turbulent flow eddies mix them.

nodes.label: Flow rate
nodes.desc: Volume of fluid passing a cross section per unit time.

nodes.label: Continuity equation
nodes.desc: Mass entering a flow tube equals mass leaving; for an incompressible fluid A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so the flow speeds up where the tube narrows.

nodes.label: Bernoulli's equation
nodes.desc: Along a streamline of an ideal fluid, pressure plus kinetic and potential energy per volume is constant; faster flow means lower pressure (Bernoulli's principle).

nodes.label: Poiseuille's law
nodes.desc: Laminar viscous flow through a tube: flow rate is the pressure difference over a resistance R = 8ηl/(πr⁴).

nodes.label: Reynolds number
nodes.desc: Dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous effects; flow in a tube is laminar below about 2000 and turbulent above about 3000.

nodes.label: Period
nodes.desc: Time for one cycle of a periodic motion (an oscillation).

nodes.label: Frequency
nodes.desc: Number of cycles per unit time; SI unit the hertz.

nodes.label: Simple harmonic oscillator
nodes.desc: A mass on an ideal spring: the restoring force is proportional to displacement, giving simple harmonic motion.

nodes.label: Harmonic oscillation
nodes.desc: The oscillator's state: amplitude A and phase shift φ about the equilibrium position; equivalently the pair (x, v) at one instant.

nodes.label: Force constant
nodes.desc: Stiffness of a spring: force per unit stretch, in N/m.

nodes.label: Restoring force
nodes.desc: Force that pushes a body back toward a stable equilibrium point; linear for small displacements.

nodes.label: Simple pendulum
nodes.desc: A point mass on a light string; for small angles it is a harmonic oscillator whose period depends only on length and g.

nodes.label: Physical pendulum
nodes.desc: An extended body swinging about a pivot; its period depends on its moment of inertia and the distance L from pivot to centre of mass.

nodes.label: Torsional pendulum
nodes.desc: A body twisting on a wire whose restoring torque is proportional to the twist angle.

nodes.label: Damped oscillator
nodes.desc: An oscillator with a drag force proportional to velocity; it is underdamped (decaying oscillation), critically damped or overdamped (no oscillation).

nodes.label: Driven oscillator and resonance
nodes.desc: A damped oscillator pushed periodically settles into motion at the driving frequency; its amplitude peaks (resonance) when the driving frequency is near the natural one.

nodes.label: Wave
nodes.desc: A disturbance that travels through a medium (mechanical wave) while each part of the medium only oscillates about its equilibrium; transverse or longitudinal.

nodes.label: Wavelength
nodes.desc: Distance between adjacent identical points of a periodic wave.

nodes.label: Wave speed
nodes.desc: Speed at which the disturbance propagates; set by the medium, not by the source.

nodes.label: Traveling wave function
nodes.desc: A wave shape that moves without changing; a pulse is a single such disturbance and y = A sin(kx − ωt + φ) is the periodic case.

nodes.label: Wave number
nodes.desc: Spatial angular frequency of a wave, in rad/m; v = ω/k.

nodes.label: Linear wave equation
nodes.desc: The equation satisfied by every wave travelling at speed v in a linear medium.

nodes.label: Wave power
nodes.desc: Energy per unit time carried by a wave; proportional to the square of the amplitude and of the frequency.

nodes.label: Intensity
nodes.desc: Power per unit area carried by a wave; for a spherical wave I = P/(4πr²).

nodes.label: Boundary conditions
nodes.desc: At a fixed end the displacement is zero and a reflected pulse is inverted; at a free end the slope is zero and the pulse returns upright.

nodes.label: Interference
nodes.desc: Two overlapping waves add constructively (in phase, double amplitude) or destructively (half a cycle apart, cancel).

nodes.label: Superposition principle
nodes.desc: When waves overlap, the displacements add; follows from the linearity of the wave equation.

nodes.label: Standing wave
nodes.desc: Two equal waves moving in opposite directions produce a pattern that does not travel: nodes stay at rest, antinodes oscillate most.

nodes.label: Normal modes
nodes.desc: A string fixed at both ends can only hold standing waves that fit its length: the fundamental and its overtones.

nodes.label: Sound wave
nodes.desc: A longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions in a medium; the pressure wave is a quarter cycle out of phase with the displacement wave.

nodes.label: Speed of sound
nodes.desc: Set by an elastic property over an inertial property of the medium: √(B/ρ) in fluids, √(Y/ρ) in solids, √(γRT/M) in an ideal gas.

nodes.label: Sound intensity level
nodes.desc: Logarithmic measure of intensity relative to the threshold I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m².

nodes.label: Air-column modes
nodes.desc: Standing sound waves in a tube: open at both ends all harmonics f_n = nv/2L; closed at one end only odd ones, f_n = nv/4L.

nodes.label: Beat frequency
nodes.desc: Two sounds of slightly different frequency produce a loudness that rises and falls at the difference frequency.

nodes.label: Doppler-shifted frequency
nodes.desc: The frequency heard changes when source or observer moves through the medium: higher when approaching, lower when receding.

nodes.label: Shock wave
nodes.desc: A source faster than sound piles up its wavefronts on a cone; the pressure jump is heard as a sonic boom, and a boat's bow wake is the surface analogue.

nodes.label: Temperature
nodes.desc: How hot a body is, read from a thermometer; bodies in thermal equilibrium share one temperature. SI unit the kelvin.

nodes.label: Thermal equilibrium
nodes.desc: The state reached by bodies in thermal contact when heat transfer between them has stopped.

nodes.label: Zeroth law
nodes.desc: Two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other.

nodes.label: Temperature scales
nodes.desc: Celsius and Fahrenheit are relative scales; the Kelvin scale is absolute, with zero at absolute zero and the triple point of water at 273.16 K.

nodes.label: Thermal expansion
nodes.desc: Most materials grow when heated: linearly in the temperature change for small changes; β ≈ 3α for isotropic solids. Water below 4 °C is an exception.

nodes.label: Thermal stress
nodes.desc: Stress that appears when a body is prevented from expanding or contracting.

nodes.label: Heat
nodes.desc: Energy transferred between bodies because of their temperature difference. 1 cal = 4.186 J (mechanical equivalent of heat).

nodes.label: Specific heat
nodes.desc: Heat needed per unit mass to raise the temperature by one kelvin.

nodes.label: Calorimetry
nodes.desc: Heat lost by the hot bodies in an insulated container equals heat gained by the cold ones.

nodes.label: Phase diagram
nodes.desc: Which phase (solid, liquid, gas) is stable at each pressure and temperature; the coexistence lines meet at the triple point and the liquid–vapor line ends at the critical point.

nodes.label: Latent heat
nodes.desc: Heat absorbed or released at constant temperature during a phase change: heat of fusion, vaporization or sublimation.

nodes.label: Heat conduction
nodes.desc: Heat flows through a material at a rate proportional to area and temperature difference and inversely to thickness.

nodes.label: Convection
nodes.desc: Heat transported by bulk motion of a fluid, driven by buoyancy (natural) or by pumps and fans (forced).

nodes.label: Stefan–Boltzmann law
nodes.desc: Every body radiates energy at a rate proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature; the net rate is σeA(T₂⁴ − T₁⁴).

nodes.label: Ideal gas law
nodes.desc: For a dilute gas, pressure times volume is proportional to the number of molecules and the absolute temperature (Boyle, Charles and Gay-Lussac combined).

nodes.label: Boltzmann constant
nodes.desc: Converts temperature to energy per molecule: 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.

nodes.label: Avogadro's number
nodes.desc: Number of molecules in one mole, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; the mole counts amount of substance.

nodes.label: Gas constant
nodes.desc: Boltzmann's constant per mole: 8.31 J/(mol·K).

nodes.label: Van der Waals equation
nodes.desc: Corrects the ideal gas law for attraction between molecules (a) and their own volume (b); predicts liquefaction below a critical temperature.

nodes.label: Equilibrium state of a gas
nodes.desc: A gas in equilibrium is fixed by two of p, V, T; the third follows from the equation of state, so the state is a point on a pV diagram.

nodes.label: Kinetic theory of gases
nodes.desc: A gas is many point molecules in random motion; pressure is the momentum they transfer to the walls in collisions.

nodes.label: Internal energy
nodes.desc: Total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules; for a monatomic ideal gas only kinetic, (3/2)Nk_BT.

nodes.label: rms speed
nodes.desc: Square root of the mean square molecular speed.

nodes.label: Dalton's law
nodes.desc: In a mixture each gas exerts its own partial pressure as if alone; the total pressure is their sum.

nodes.label: Mean free path
nodes.desc: Average distance a molecule travels between collisions; divided by the mean speed it gives the mean free time.

nodes.label: Molar heat capacity at constant volume
nodes.desc: Heat per mole per kelvin at fixed volume.

nodes.label: Equipartition theorem
nodes.desc: In thermal equilibrium each quadratic term in a molecule's energy (degree of freedom) carries an average energy ½k_BT.

nodes.label: Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution
nodes.desc: The equilibrium distribution of molecular speeds in an ideal gas.

nodes.label: Most probable speed
nodes.desc: Speed at the peak of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution; below the mean and rms speeds.

nodes.label: Thermodynamic system
nodes.desc: A part of the world separated by a boundary from its surroundings (environment); closed if no matter crosses, open otherwise. In equilibrium a few variables describe it.

nodes.label: Equation of state
nodes.desc: A relation among the state variables of a system in equilibrium.

nodes.label: Quasi-static process
nodes.desc: A process slow enough that the system passes through a sequence of equilibrium states, so it is a curve on the pV diagram.

nodes.label: Work done by a gas
nodes.desc: Work done by a system that changes volume; the area under the path on the pV diagram, so it depends on the path.

nodes.label: First law of thermodynamics
nodes.desc: The change of internal energy equals the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system.

nodes.label: Thermodynamic processes
nodes.desc: Paths with one quantity held fixed: T (isothermal), p (isobaric), V (isochoric), or no heat exchanged (adiabatic); a cyclic process returns to its start. A reversible process can be run backward through the same states.

nodes.label: Molar heat capacity at constant pressure
nodes.desc: Heat per mole per kelvin at fixed pressure; larger than C_V because the gas also does work.

nodes.label: Adiabatic process of an ideal gas
nodes.desc: In a quasi-static adiabatic expansion the gas cools; pressure and volume follow pV^γ = constant with γ = C_p/C_V.

nodes.label: Irreversible process
nodes.desc: A process that cannot be undone without leaving a change in the surroundings: friction, free expansion, heat flow across a finite temperature difference.

nodes.label: Clausius statement
nodes.desc: Heat never flows spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body; doing so requires work.

nodes.label: Heat engine
nodes.desc: A device run in a cycle that takes heat Q_h from a hot reservoir, rejects Q_c to a cold reservoir and delivers the difference as work.

nodes.label: Efficiency
nodes.desc: Fraction of the heat taken in that is turned into work.

nodes.label: Refrigerator and heat pump
nodes.desc: An engine run backward: work moves heat from a cold reservoir to a hot one, to cool the cold side (refrigerator) or heat the hot side (heat pump).

nodes.label: Coefficient of performance
nodes.desc: Heat moved per work supplied; can exceed 1.

nodes.label: Kelvin statement
nodes.desc: No cyclic process can convert heat from one reservoir entirely into work; equivalently there is no perfect engine (and, by the Clausius form, no perfect refrigerator).

nodes.label: Carnot cycle
nodes.desc: A reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic steps between two reservoirs; an engine run on it is a Carnot engine.

nodes.label: Carnot principle
nodes.desc: No engine between two reservoirs beats a reversible one, and all reversible engines between them have e = 1 − T_c/T_h.

nodes.label: Entropy
nodes.desc: A state function whose change is the heat added reversibly divided by the absolute temperature.

nodes.label: Second law (entropy statement)
nodes.desc: The entropy of an isolated system never decreases; it stays constant only for reversible processes.

nodes.label: Third law
nodes.desc: Entropy changes along an isotherm vanish as the temperature approaches absolute zero; absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.

nodes.label: Electric charge
nodes.desc: A property of matter that comes in two signs: like charges repel, unlike attract. Additive; SI unit the coulomb.

nodes.label: Conservation of charge
nodes.desc: The total charge of an isolated system never changes; charging a body only moves charge from one body to another.

nodes.label: Charge carriers
nodes.desc: Ordinary charge is carried by electrons (−e) and protons (+e); neutrons are neutral. An ion has more or fewer electrons than protons.

nodes.label: Conductor
nodes.desc: A material in which some electrons (conduction electrons) move freely; charge placed on it spreads out, and nearby charges can induce a separation (charging by induction).

nodes.label: Insulator
nodes.desc: A material whose charges are bound to atoms; a field can only shift them slightly, polarizing the material into small dipoles.

nodes.label: Coulomb's law
nodes.desc: Two point charges exert forces on each other along the line joining them, proportional to the product of the charges and inversely to the square of the distance.

nodes.label: Permittivity of vacuum
nodes.desc: Constant in Coulomb's law, 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²); k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².

nodes.label: Superposition of electric forces
nodes.desc: The force from several charges is the vector sum of the forces each would exert alone.

nodes.label: Point-charge configuration
nodes.desc: The simplest electrostatic state: which charges there are and where they sit.

nodes.label: Electric field
nodes.desc: The field produced by source charges, defined at every point of space; a test charge there feels qE⃗.

nodes.label: Field value
nodes.desc: Force per unit test charge at a point; measured with a small test charge.

nodes.label: Continuous charge distribution
nodes.desc: Charge spread along a line, over a surface or through a volume, described by a charge density; an infinite straight wire and an infinite plane are idealised cases.

nodes.label: Field lines
nodes.desc: Curves drawn tangent to the field, starting on positive and ending on negative charges, more crowded where the field is stronger.

nodes.label: Electric dipole moment
nodes.desc: Charge times separation of a ± charge pair; molecules can have a permanent dipole or one induced by a field.

nodes.label: Electric flux
nodes.desc: The amount of field passing through a surface: field component along the area vector (normal to the surface) times area, summed over the surface.

nodes.label: Gauss's law
nodes.desc: The electric flux through any closed (Gaussian) surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀.

nodes.label: Symmetry method
nodes.desc: With spherical, cylindrical or planar symmetry the field is constant on a well-chosen Gaussian surface, and Gauss's law gives it directly.

nodes.label: Conductor in electrostatic equilibrium
nodes.desc: With charges at rest, the field inside a conductor is zero, excess charge sits on the surface, and just outside E = σ/ε₀ perpendicular to the surface.

nodes.label: Electric potential energy
nodes.desc: Potential energy of a system of charges; the Coulomb force is conservative, so it exists.

nodes.label: Electric potential
nodes.desc: Potential energy per unit charge at each point; a scalar field defined up to an additive constant.

nodes.label: Voltage
nodes.desc: Potential difference between two points, measured with a voltmeter; SI unit the volt. qΔV is an energy (electron-volt for q = e).

nodes.label: Gradient
nodes.desc: The vector of partial derivatives of a scalar field; points toward steepest increase.

nodes.label: Equipotential surfaces
nodes.desc: Surfaces of constant potential; the field is perpendicular to them and no work is done moving a charge along one. A conductor's surface is one; grounding sets it to zero.

nodes.label: Capacitor
nodes.desc: Two conductors carrying equal and opposite charges, often separated by a dielectric; the parallel-plate capacitor is the standard example.

nodes.label: Capacitance
nodes.desc: Charge stored per volt of potential difference; depends only on geometry and the material between the conductors. SI unit the farad.

nodes.label: Capacitors in series and parallel
nodes.desc: Capacitors in parallel share a voltage and their capacitances add; in series they share a charge and the inverses add.

nodes.label: Energy stored in a capacitor
nodes.desc: Work needed to charge a capacitor, stored in its electric field.

nodes.label: Electric energy density
nodes.desc: Energy per unit volume stored in an electric field.

nodes.label: Dielectric constant
nodes.desc: Factor by which an insulating material between the plates raises the capacitance and lowers the field.

nodes.label: Molecular model of a dielectric
nodes.desc: The applied field induces or aligns molecular dipoles; the induced surface charges create an induced field that partly cancels the applied one.

nodes.label: Dielectric strength
nodes.desc: Largest field an insulator withstands before it breaks down and conducts.

nodes.label: Electric current
nodes.desc: Rate at which charge passes a cross section; SI unit the ampere (1 A = 1 C/s). Conventional current points the way positive charge would move.

nodes.label: Electric circuit
nodes.desc: A closed conducting path through sources and elements, drawn as a schematic; charge flows steadily only around closed paths.

nodes.label: Drift velocity
nodes.desc: Small average velocity of the charge carriers along a wire, superposed on their fast random motion.

nodes.label: Current density
nodes.desc: Current per unit area at each point of a conductor; integrated over a cross section it gives the current.

nodes.label: Resistivity
nodes.desc: Material property: field needed per unit current density; its inverse is the electrical conductivity. It grows roughly linearly with temperature in metals.

nodes.label: Resistance
nodes.desc: Voltage per current of a component; for a uniform wire R = ρL/A. SI unit the ohm.

nodes.label: Ohm's law
nodes.desc: For many materials current is proportional to voltage with R independent of V (ohmic); devices such as diodes are nonohmic.

nodes.label: Electric power
nodes.desc: Rate at which electrical energy is delivered to an element; in a resistor it becomes heat at I²R = V²/R.

nodes.label: Superconducting state
nodes.desc: Below a critical temperature some materials lose all resistance and expel magnetic fields (Meissner effect); a quantum effect of electron pairs.

nodes.label: Electromotive force
nodes.desc: Work per unit charge done by a source (battery, generator) in moving charge around a circuit; the voltage of the source with no current.

nodes.label: Terminal voltage
nodes.desc: Voltage across a source's terminals; below its emf by the potential drop on its internal resistance.

nodes.label: Resistors in series and parallel
nodes.desc: Resistors in series carry the same current and their resistances add; in parallel they share the voltage and the inverses add.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's rules
nodes.desc: Junction rule: current into a junction equals current out. Loop rule: the potential differences around any closed loop sum to zero.

nodes.label: Ammeter and voltmeter
nodes.desc: An ammeter is placed in series and has very small resistance; a voltmeter is placed in parallel and has very large resistance, so neither disturbs the circuit much.

nodes.label: RC circuit
nodes.desc: A capacitor charging or discharging through a resistor: charge and current change exponentially with time constant τ = RC.

nodes.label: Magnetic poles
nodes.desc: Every magnet has a north and a south pole; like poles repel, unlike attract, and cutting a magnet never isolates a single pole.

nodes.label: Magnetic force on a moving charge
nodes.desc: A charge moving through a magnetic field feels a force perpendicular to both its velocity and the field (right-hand rule); the force does no work.

nodes.label: Magnetic field
nodes.desc: The field around magnets and currents, mapped by a compass; its field lines form closed loops. SI unit the tesla (1 G = 10⁻⁴ T).

nodes.label: Magnetic field value
nodes.desc: Field at one point, defined through the force on a moving test charge: B = F/(qv sin θ).

nodes.label: Circular and helical orbits
nodes.desc: A charge in a uniform field moves on a circle of radius mv/(qB) with period 2πm/(qB); a velocity component along B⃗ turns the circle into a helix.

nodes.label: Magnetic dipole moment
nodes.desc: Current times area of a loop (times the number of turns), along the loop's normal; a current loop is a magnetic dipole.

nodes.label: Hall voltage
nodes.desc: Voltage across a current-carrying strip in a magnetic field, from carriers pushed to one side; its sign reveals the sign of the carriers.

nodes.label: Velocity selector
nodes.desc: Crossed electric and magnetic fields pass undeflected only particles with speed E/B.

nodes.label: Biot–Savart law
nodes.desc: Each element of a current contributes to the magnetic field in proportion to the current and inversely to the square of the distance, perpendicular to both element and line of sight.

nodes.label: Permeability of free space
nodes.desc: Constant in the magnetic field laws, 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A.

nodes.label: Field of a long straight wire
nodes.desc: Circles around the wire, falling inversely with distance (right-hand rule for its direction).

nodes.label: Force between parallel currents
nodes.desc: Parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel; this force once defined the ampere.

nodes.label: Ampère's law
nodes.desc: The line integral of the magnetic field around any closed loop equals μ₀ times the current through it.

nodes.label: Solenoid and toroid
nodes.desc: A long coil has a nearly uniform field inside, B = μ₀nI, and almost none outside; a toroid confines its field, B = μ₀NI/(2πr).

nodes.label: Magnetism in matter
nodes.desc: Atomic magnetic dipoles respond to a field: weakly along it (paramagnetic, χ > 0), weakly against it (diamagnetic, χ < 0), or strongly with domains and hysteresis (ferromagnetic).

nodes.label: Magnetic flux
nodes.desc: Amount of magnetic field through a surface; SI unit the weber.

nodes.label: Faraday's law
nodes.desc: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf in it, whether the field, the area or the orientation changes.

nodes.label: Lenz's law
nodes.desc: The induced emf drives a current whose magnetic field opposes the change of flux that produced it.

nodes.label: Motional emf
nodes.desc: Emf in a conductor moving through a magnetic field.

nodes.label: Induced electric field
nodes.desc: A changing magnetic field creates an electric field whose lines close on themselves; it is not conservative.

nodes.label: Eddy currents
nodes.desc: Currents induced in a conductor moving in, or exposed to, a changing magnetic field; by Lenz's law they oppose the motion (magnetic damping).

nodes.label: Electric generator
nodes.desc: A coil turning in a magnetic field produces a sinusoidal emf with peak NBAω; a motor's coil produces the same, called back emf.

nodes.label: Mutual inductance
nodes.desc: Flux through one circuit per current in another; a changing current in one induces emf ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt in the other. SI unit the henry.

nodes.label: Self-inductance
nodes.desc: A coil's own flux per unit of its current; a changing current induces ε = −L dI/dt that opposes the change. An inductor is a coil built for this.

nodes.label: Energy in an inductor
nodes.desc: Work done against the back emf while the current builds up, stored in the magnetic field.

nodes.label: Magnetic energy density
nodes.desc: Energy per unit volume stored in a magnetic field.

nodes.label: RL circuit
nodes.desc: Current in a resistor–inductor circuit rises or decays exponentially with time constant τ_L = L/R.

nodes.label: LC circuit
nodes.desc: Charge sloshes between a capacitor and an inductor; energy passes between electric and magnetic fields.

nodes.label: RLC circuit
nodes.desc: Adding resistance damps the LC oscillation: underdamped, critically damped or overdamped as for a mechanical oscillator.

nodes.label: Alternating source
nodes.desc: A source whose voltage (and current) reverses periodically; direct current (dc) flows one way only.

nodes.label: Phasors
nodes.desc: Represents a sinusoid A sin(ωt + φ) as a vector of length A rotating at ω; sinusoids of one frequency add as vectors.

nodes.label: Capacitive reactance
nodes.desc: Opposition of a capacitor to alternating current; current leads voltage by 90°.

nodes.label: rms current and voltage
nodes.desc: Effective values of a sinusoid: the dc values that deliver the same average power.

nodes.label: Inductive reactance
nodes.desc: Opposition of an inductor to alternating current; current lags voltage by 90°.

nodes.label: Impedance and phase angle
nodes.desc: Total opposition of a series RLC circuit to ac, I₀ = V₀/Z; the phase angle φ = tan⁻¹((X_L − X_C)/R) is how far current lags voltage.

nodes.label: Average ac power
nodes.desc: Power averaged over a cycle; only the resistor dissipates, and cos φ is the power factor.

nodes.label: AC resonance
nodes.desc: Current in a series RLC circuit peaks when X_L = X_C; the quality factor measures how sharp the peak is (bandwidth Δω = ω₀/Q).

nodes.label: Transformer
nodes.desc: Two coils on one iron core: the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, and the current ratio its inverse, so power is transmitted at high voltage and low current.

nodes.label: Maxwell's equations
nodes.desc: Gauss's law for E⃗, Gauss's law for B⃗ (no monopoles), Faraday's law, and Ampère's law with Maxwell's displacement current; with the Lorentz force they complete classical electromagnetism.

nodes.label: Displacement current
nodes.desc: Maxwell's term: a changing electric flux acts like a current in Ampère's law, needed where a capacitor interrupts the conduction current.

nodes.label: Electromagnetic field
nodes.desc: The dynamical state of classical electromagnetism: electric and magnetic fields at every point and time, evolving by Maxwell's equations.

nodes.label: Plane electromagnetic wave
nodes.desc: A solution of Maxwell's equations in empty space: transverse electric and magnetic fields in phase, travelling at c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀).

nodes.label: Poynting vector
nodes.desc: Energy flux of the electromagnetic field: energy per unit area per unit time, along the direction of propagation.

nodes.label: Radiation pressure
nodes.desc: Pressure exerted by light because electromagnetic waves carry momentum U/c.

nodes.label: Electromagnetic spectrum
nodes.desc: Electromagnetic waves of all wavelengths: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, distinguished only by frequency.

nodes.label: Index of refraction
nodes.desc: Ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a medium; at least 1.

nodes.label: Ray model of light
nodes.desc: Geometric optics: light travels along straight rays in a uniform medium, bending only at boundaries. Valid when objects and apertures are much larger than the wavelength.

nodes.label: Law of reflection
nodes.desc: A ray reflects from a smooth surface at the same angle to the normal as it arrived, in the same plane.

nodes.label: Law of refraction
nodes.desc: A ray entering a medium of different index bends toward the normal if the new index is larger (Snell's law).

nodes.label: Critical angle
nodes.desc: Angle of incidence beyond which light going into a medium of lower index is totally reflected (total internal reflection).

nodes.label: Dispersion
nodes.desc: The index of refraction depends on wavelength, so a prism spreads white light into colours.

nodes.label: Huygens's principle
nodes.desc: Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets; the new wavefront is their envelope. It explains reflection, refraction and diffraction (wave optics).

nodes.label: Polarization
nodes.desc: The direction of the electric field of light in the plane perpendicular to its travel: fixed for polarized light (vertically, horizontally…), random for unpolarized light.

nodes.label: Malus's law
nodes.desc: A polarizing filter transmits the field component along its axis, so intensity falls as cos²θ.

nodes.label: Brewster's angle
nodes.desc: Angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely polarized parallel to the surface.

nodes.label: Optical image
nodes.desc: Where rays from a point of an object meet (real image, can be caught on a screen) or appear to come from (virtual image). A plane mirror forms a virtual image as far behind as the object is in front.

nodes.label: Mirror equation
nodes.desc: For a curved (spherical) mirror and rays near the optical axis, object and image distances are related through the focal length f = R/2.

nodes.label: Magnification
nodes.desc: Image height over object height; negative for an inverted image.

nodes.label: Aberrations
nodes.desc: Real mirrors and lenses do not bring all rays to one point: spherical aberration (rays far from the axis), coma (off-axis points), and others.

nodes.label: Refraction at a curved surface
nodes.desc: A single spherical boundary between media forms images; for a flat boundary it gives the apparent depth h_i = (n₂/n₁)h_o.

nodes.label: Thin lens
nodes.desc: Two refracting surfaces close together: converging lenses (f > 0) and diverging lenses (f < 0), with 1/f = (n₂/n₁ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) (lens maker's equation). Images are found by ray tracing.

nodes.label: The eye as an optical system
nodes.desc: The eye images onto the retina at fixed distance by changing its power (accommodation) between the near and far points; myopia and hyperopia are corrected with lenses.

nodes.label: Optical power
nodes.desc: Inverse focal length in diopters (m⁻¹); powers of thin lenses in contact add.

nodes.label: Angular magnification
nodes.desc: How much larger an object appears through an instrument than to the unaided eye at the near point; a simple magnifier gives at most 1 + 25 cm/f.

nodes.label: Microscope and telescope
nodes.desc: Two-lens instruments: the objective forms a real image that the eyepiece magnifies; magnifications multiply.

nodes.label: Coherent light
nodes.desc: Light waves whose phase difference stays constant (coherent), usually of one wavelength (monochromatic); incoherent light washes out interference.

nodes.label: Double-slit interference
nodes.desc: Young's experiment: light from two slits forms bright fringes where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths (order m) and dark fringes halfway between.

nodes.label: Multiple-slit interference
nodes.desc: With N slits the principal maxima stay at d sin θ = mλ but become sharper, with N − 2 weak secondary maxima between them.

nodes.label: Thin-film interference
nodes.desc: Light reflected from the top and bottom of a thin film interferes; a half-wavelength phase change on reflection from a higher-index medium decides which colours are reinforced (soap bubbles, Newton's rings).

nodes.label: Michelson interferometer
nodes.desc: Splits a beam, sends the halves along two arms and recombines them; moving one mirror by λ/2 shifts the pattern by one fringe.

nodes.label: Single-slit diffraction
nodes.desc: Light spreads after passing a narrow slit; wavelets from different parts of the slit cancel at angles where a sin θ = mλ.

nodes.label: Single-slit intensity
nodes.desc: Intensity across the single-slit pattern, β = πa sin θ/λ; the central peak's width is set by λ/a.

nodes.label: Two-slit diffraction pattern
nodes.desc: With slits of finite width, the double-slit fringes are modulated by the single-slit envelope; fringes falling on envelope minima are missing orders.

nodes.label: Diffraction grating
nodes.desc: Thousands of equally spaced slits give very sharp principal maxima, so a grating separates wavelengths precisely.

nodes.label: Rayleigh criterion
nodes.desc: Two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other; diffraction limits every optical instrument's resolution.

nodes.label: Bragg's law
nodes.desc: X-rays reflected from successive planes of atoms in a crystal (Bragg planes) interfere constructively when the extra path 2d sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths.

nodes.label: Holography
nodes.desc: A hologram records the interference of object light with a reference beam, storing amplitude and phase; illuminated again, it reconstructs a three-dimensional image.

nodes.label: Special relativity
nodes.desc: Einstein's theory of space and time for inertial frames, built on two postulates; it reconciles mechanics with electromagnetism.

nodes.label: First postulate
nodes.desc: The laws of physics, including electromagnetism, have the same form in every inertial frame.

nodes.label: Michelson–Morley result
nodes.desc: An interferometer turned relative to Earth's motion showed no change in the speed of light: there is no detectable motion through an ether.

nodes.label: Second postulate
nodes.desc: Light in vacuum travels at c in every inertial frame, whatever the motion of source or observer.

nodes.label: Relativity of simultaneity
nodes.desc: Two events simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally not simultaneous in another moving relative to it.

nodes.label: Time dilation
nodes.desc: A clock moving relative to an observer runs slow: the time between two events at one place in the clock's frame (proper time Δτ) is the shortest.

nodes.label: Lorentz factor
nodes.desc: Factor that measures how far relativistic effects depart from Newtonian ones; 1 at rest, infinite at c.

nodes.label: Length contraction
nodes.desc: A body is longest in its own rest frame (proper length L₀); measured while it moves, it is shorter along the motion, L = L₀/γ.

nodes.label: Lorentz transformation
nodes.desc: Converts the coordinates of an event between two inertial frames so that the speed of light is the same in both.

nodes.label: Space-time
nodes.desc: The four-dimensional arena of special relativity; a particle's history is a world line, and the interval between events is the same in all frames.

nodes.label: Relativistic velocity addition
nodes.desc: Velocities combine so that no sum of speeds below c ever exceeds c; for slow speeds this reduces to classical (Galilean) velocity addition.

nodes.label: Relativistic Doppler effect
nodes.desc: The frequency of light from a receding source is lower (red shift), from an approaching one higher; it depends only on the relative velocity.

nodes.label: Relativistic momentum
nodes.desc: The momentum conserved in all inertial frames; m is the rest mass, the same in every frame.

nodes.label: Relativistic kinetic energy
nodes.desc: Work needed to bring a body from rest to speed u; it grows without bound as u → c, so no massive body reaches c.

nodes.label: Total energy and rest energy
nodes.desc: Total energy of a body: kinetic energy plus its rest energy mc²; mass is a form of energy. E² = (pc)² + (mc²)².

nodes.label: Blackbody radiation
nodes.desc: Radiation in equilibrium with a perfect absorber and emitter at temperature T; its spectrum depends only on T, peaking at λ_max with λ_max T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K (Wien).

nodes.label: Planck's constant
nodes.desc: The quantum of action, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; it sets the scale at which energy comes in discrete amounts.

nodes.label: Planck's hypothesis
nodes.desc: The oscillators exchanging energy with cavity radiation can only have energies that are whole multiples of hf.

nodes.label: Photoelectron energy
nodes.desc: Light on a metal ejects photoelectrons (photocurrent from the photoelectrode); their maximum kinetic energy is measured by the stopping potential.

nodes.label: Cut-off frequency
nodes.desc: Below a cut-off frequency (above a cut-off wavelength) no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.

nodes.label: Photon
nodes.desc: A quantum of the electromagnetic field: energy hf, momentum h/λ along the propagation vector, zero rest mass. The photoelectric effect is a quantum phenomenon.

nodes.label: Work function
nodes.desc: Minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal's surface.

nodes.label: Compton shift
nodes.desc: X-rays scattered by electrons come out with longer wavelength, by an amount fixed by the scattering angle; λ_c = h/(m₀c) = 0.00243 nm is the Compton wavelength.

nodes.label: Hydrogen line spectrum
nodes.desc: Hydrogen emits and absorbs only at discrete wavelengths (Fraunhofer lines in sunlight), in series named Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund and Humphreys.

nodes.label: Nuclear model of the atom
nodes.desc: Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed that nearly all of an atom's mass and its positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus, with electrons far outside.

nodes.label: Bohr's model
nodes.desc: Postulates for hydrogen: the electron moves only on orbits with angular momentum nħ, does not radiate on them, and emits or absorbs a photon when it jumps between them.

nodes.label: Hydrogen energy levels
nodes.desc: The allowed states of Bohr's atom: radii r_n = a₀n² (Bohr radius a₀ = 0.529 Å) and energies −E₀/n²; ground state −13.6 eV, ionization energy 13.6 eV. Hydrogen-like ions scale with Z.

nodes.label: de Broglie's hypothesis
nodes.desc: Every particle has an associated matter wave (de Broglie wave) with wavelength h/p; the wave packet moves at the group velocity, which equals the particle's velocity.

nodes.label: Electron diffraction
nodes.desc: Davisson and Germer saw electrons diffracted by a nickel crystal with the angles of Bragg's law, confirming λ = h/p.

nodes.label: Wave–particle duality
nodes.desc: Light and matter both show wave behaviour (interference in the double-slit interference experiment) and particle behaviour (single detections); neither picture alone suffices.

nodes.label: Uncertainty principle
nodes.desc: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp: the product of their uncertainties is at least ħ/2.

nodes.label: Wave function
nodes.desc: The quantum state of a particle: a complex function of position and time; its symmetry under x → −x may be even or odd.

nodes.label: Born rule
nodes.desc: |Ψ(x, t)|² is the probability density for finding the particle at x; the total probability is one (normalization condition).

nodes.label: Measurement and state reduction
nodes.desc: A measurement gives one definite outcome, and the wave function is then replaced by one consistent with it (wave function collapse, Copenhagen interpretation).

nodes.label: Expectation value
nodes.desc: Average of many measurements on identically prepared systems; position and momentum act as operators x and −iħ ∂/∂x.

nodes.label: Correspondence principle
nodes.desc: In the limit of large energies (large quantum numbers) quantum predictions agree with classical mechanics.

nodes.label: Wave packet
nodes.desc: A localised wave made by superposing plane waves of nearby wave numbers; the narrower it is in x, the broader in k.

nodes.label: Energy–time uncertainty
nodes.desc: A state that lasts only Δt has an energy spread at least ħ/(2Δt); short-lived states have broad lines.

nodes.label: Schrödinger equation
nodes.desc: The equation of motion of the wave function: given Ψ at one time and the potential energy U, it fixes Ψ at all times.

nodes.label: Time-independent Schrödinger equation
nodes.desc: For a potential that does not change in time, Ψ = ψ(x)e^{−iωt}; ψ satisfies an eigenvalue equation for the energy, and e^{−iωt} is the time-modulation factor.

nodes.label: Particle in a box
nodes.desc: A particle confined to an infinite square well: ψ_n = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), standing matter waves; only discrete energy levels with quantum number n ≥ 1 are allowed, so even the ground state energy is nonzero.

nodes.label: Stationary state
nodes.desc: A solution with one definite energy; its probability density does not change, so it is a standing wave state.

nodes.label: Quantum harmonic oscillator
nodes.desc: The Schrödinger equation with U = ½mω²x²: equally spaced levels, a zero-point energy ħω/2, and wave functions built from Hermite polynomials.

nodes.label: Tunneling probability
nodes.desc: A particle can cross a potential barrier higher than its energy; the transmission probability falls exponentially with barrier width and with √(U₀ − E).

nodes.label: Hydrogen atom
nodes.desc: Solutions of the Schrödinger equation for the Coulomb potential: atomic orbitals labelled by n, l (0 … n − 1) and m (−l … l). Energies depend only on n and agree with Bohr's; electrons have no definite orbits.

nodes.label: Quantized angular momentum
nodes.desc: Magnitude and one component of orbital angular momentum take only discrete values.

nodes.label: Orbital magnetic moment
nodes.desc: The orbiting electron is a current loop; its moment comes in units of the Bohr magneton μ_B = eħ/2m_e.

nodes.label: Zeeman effect
nodes.desc: In a magnetic field, levels with different m split, and spectral lines split into several components.

nodes.label: Electron spin
nodes.desc: Intrinsic angular momentum of the electron, s = ½ with m_s = ±½, shown by the two beams of the Stern–Gerlach experiment; it carries a magnetic moment μ⃗_s ≈ −(e/m_e)S⃗, antiparallel to the spin because the electron's charge is negative.

nodes.label: Spin–orbit and hyperfine coupling
nodes.desc: The electron's spin moment interacts with the field of its orbital motion (fine structure) and with the nuclear spin (hyperfine structure, spin-flip transitions such as hydrogen's 21-cm line).

nodes.label: Pauli exclusion principle
nodes.desc: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, m_s).

nodes.label: Electron configuration
nodes.desc: Electrons fill subshells in order of energy, each with at most 4l + 2; the outermost (valence) electrons fix chemical groups and the transition metals.

nodes.label: Selection rules
nodes.desc: Atomic transitions that emit or absorb a photon change l by one, because the photon carries one unit of angular momentum.

nodes.label: Atomic X-rays
nodes.desc: Heavy atoms emit characteristic X-ray lines when an inner vacancy is filled, with frequencies following Moseley's law; a continuous braking-radiation spectrum accompanies them.

nodes.label: Laser
nodes.desc: An incoming photon stimulates an excited atom to emit an identical photon; with more atoms in an excited metastable state than below it (population inversion) the light is amplified into coherent, monochromatic light.

nodes.label: Molecular bonds
nodes.desc: Atoms bind by transferring an electron (ionic bond, energy set by ionization energy, electron affinity and Coulomb attraction), by sharing a pair of electrons in an antisymmetric spin state (covalent bond, exchange symmetry, hybridization), or by induced dipo…

nodes.label: Molecular energy levels
nodes.desc: A diatomic molecule rotates and vibrates with quantized energies; electric dipole transitions obey Δl = ±1 and Δn = ±1, giving band spectra.

nodes.label: Crystal lattice
nodes.desc: Atoms or ions in a solid arranged in a repeating lattice (simple cubic, body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic); the Madelung constant sums the Coulomb energy of an ionic crystal, and a repulsion constant sets the short-range repulsion.

nodes.label: Free electron gas
nodes.desc: Conduction electrons as particles in a three-dimensional box, filling the lowest states two per level (exclusion principle) up to the Fermi energy; occupation at temperature T follows the Fermi factor.

nodes.label: Energy bands
nodes.desc: In a crystal the atomic levels broaden into energy bands separated by energy gaps; a filled valence band with a large gap gives an insulator, a small gap a semiconductor, a partly filled band a conductor.

nodes.label: Doped semiconductor
nodes.desc: Impurity atoms add donor levels (n-type, extra electrons) or acceptor levels (p-type, holes) in the gap; the majority carrier sets the type, and the Hall effect shows its sign.

nodes.label: p–n junction
nodes.desc: Joining p- and n-type material creates a depletion layer with a built-in field; current flows easily in forward bias and hardly at all in reverse bias, until breakdown.

nodes.label: Junction transistor
nodes.desc: Two junctions back to back: a small base current controls a large collector current, so the device amplifies.

nodes.label: Critical magnetic field
nodes.desc: Field above which superconductivity is destroyed; type I superconductors switch abruptly, type II pass through a mixed state.

nodes.label: BCS theory
nodes.desc: Lattice vibrations bind electrons into Cooper pairs, which condense into one quantum state that carries current without resistance.

nodes.label: Nuclide
nodes.desc: A nucleus specified by its atomic number Z (protons) and neutron number N; mass number A = Z + N counts nucleons. Isotopes share Z. Radius r = r₀A^{1/3}; masses in atomic mass units.

nodes.label: Strong nuclear force
nodes.desc: Attraction between nucleons, much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion at about 1 fm but negligible beyond a few fm.

nodes.label: Binding energy
nodes.desc: Energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons, equal to the mass defect times c²; binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron.

nodes.label: Radioactive decay law
nodes.desc: Unstable nuclei decay at random with a constant probability λ per unit time, so their number and activity fall exponentially: half-life T½ = 0.693/λ, mean lifetime 1/λ.

nodes.label: Radioactive dating
nodes.desc: Ages from the fraction of a radioactive isotope left, as in carbon-14 dating of once-living material.

nodes.label: Nuclear decays
nodes.desc: A parent nucleus becomes a daughter: α decay emits a helium nucleus, β⁻ decay an electron and an antineutrino, β⁺ decay a positron (antielectron) and a neutrino, γ decay a photon from an excited nucleus. Heavy nuclei decay in series; transuranic elements are…

nodes.label: Fission
nodes.desc: A heavy nucleus such as ²³⁵U splits after absorbing a neutron, releasing about 200 MeV and further neutrons; a chain reaction is critical when each fission causes one more on average (critical mass).

nodes.label: Liquid drop model
nodes.desc: Treats the nucleus as a drop of incompressible nuclear fluid held by surface tension (strong force) and pushed apart by Coulomb repulsion; deformation splits a heavy drop.

nodes.label: Fusion
nodes.desc: Light nuclei combine and release energy; in the Sun four protons become helium by the proton–proton chain. Stars build heavier elements (nucleosynthesis).

nodes.label: Radiation dose
nodes.desc: Energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue (rad), weighted by the relative biological effectiveness of the radiation to give the equivalent dose (rem, sievert).

nodes.label: Fundamental forces
nodes.desc: Four fundamental forces, each carried by bosons: gluons (strong), photons (electromagnetic), W and Z bosons (weak), gravitons (gravity, unobserved). The electromagnetic and weak forces unify into the electroweak force; grand unified theories and a theory of e…

nodes.label: Elementary particles
nodes.desc: Matter is made of fermions (half-integer spin): leptons such as the electron and neutrino, and quarks, which form hadrons (baryons from three quarks, mesons from a quark and an antiquark). Every particle has an antiparticle, such as the positron. Bosons carry…

nodes.label: Particle conservation laws
nodes.desc: Reactions conserve charge, baryon number and lepton number; strangeness is conserved by the strong and electromagnetic forces but not the weak force.

nodes.label: Quark model
nodes.desc: Hadrons are built from quarks with fractional charges; a new quantum number, color, lets three identical quarks share a state, and only colourless combinations exist.

nodes.label: Standard Model
nodes.desc: The theory of the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces: forces arise from the exchange of virtual particles, pictured in Feynman diagrams; quantum electrodynamics (QED) and quantum chromodynamics (QCD) are its parts.

nodes.label: Hubble's law
nodes.desc: Distant galaxies recede with speeds proportional to their distance, measured from the redshift of their light; H₀ is Hubble's constant.

nodes.label: Big Bang model
nodes.desc: The universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense early state; cosmology studies this history.

nodes.label: Cosmic microwave background
